keyVerseText: And with them their brethren of the second degree, Zechariah, Ben, and Jaaziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, Eliab, and Benaiah, and Maaseiah, and Mattithiah, and Elipheleh, and Mikneiah, and Obededom, and Jeiel, the porters.
rootMeaning: The root of מַעֲשֵׂיָה (Maʻăsêyâh) is מַעֲשֶׂה (maʻăseh), which denotes an act, deed, or work, combined with the divine element יָהּ (Jah), a shortened form of the name of God. Thus, the name literally means "work of Jehovah." This etymology highlights not just any work but one that is divinely appointed or connected to God's purpose, adding a layer of sacred intentionality beyond the common English gloss of a personal name.
usageInScripture: The word מַעֲשֵׂיָה appears 23 times in Scripture, predominantly as a proper name, Maaseiah, referring to sixteen different Israelites. The top translations consistently render it as "Maaseiah" or variants thereof, indicating its primary use as a personal name rather than a common noun. This consistent translation underscores its identity as a person linked to God's work rather than a general concept of labor or deed.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מַעֲשֵׂיָה as "work of Jehovah" enriches our appreciation of the individuals bearing this name as those whose lives or roles were connected to God's purposes. It reminds believers that our actions and callings are ultimately rooted in God's sovereign work. The recurrence of this name among priests and leaders in post-exilic Israel emphasizes the importance of faithfulness to God's covenant and law. For the Christian faith, it points to the continuity of God's redemptive work through His people, foreshadowing Christ as the ultimate fulfillment of God's work among humanity.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 15:18, Maaseiah is listed among the brethren who assisted in the sacred task of bringing the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem. The use of the name here highlights that those involved were not random individuals but people connected to God's work. Maaseiah's presence among the porters symbolizes faithful service in God's divine plan, reminding us that every role in God's kingdom contributes to His redemptive purpose.
